newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish bank merger needed soon - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Swedish bank merger needed soon - analysts.

text.p: Expectations of a merger between Swedish banks S-E-Banken and Nordbanken have reached fever pitch and bank shares could tumble if a merger is not announced shortly.
"If nothing happens this week, the shares could fall," said Jonny Sylven, analyst at Swedish bank Swedbank. "Many market players are worried and they do not know what to do."

Shares in the banks have surged since last autumn on speculation about sector restructuring and hopes were further fuelled when banking group Handelsbanken placed a bid in late 1996 for mortgage bank Stadshypotek.

Recurrent media reports have kept rumours alive and on Thursday Swedish financial daily Finanstidningen said a merger might not be announced until February 18 when both banks have will have released 1996 earnings.

Some analysts do not expect the shares to fall back before Nordbanken has released its earnings on that date, following S-E-Banken's report on February 14. Others see investors prepared to wait for an announcement for quite some time.

"Investors can afford to wait, but speculative buyers might lose interest," said Keith Baird, analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in London. "But you probably have a lot of U.S. long-term investors and they are not likely to leave."
Because neigher bank could afford to buy the other outright analysts believe in a merger of equals, thereby avoiding building up goodwill in the accounts which would have to be written off later.
The dark horse is the state's 59 percent Nordbanken stake.

Some analysts worry that the Social Democrat government will not approve a merger as it is likely to lead to lay-offs, aggravating an already high unemployment level in Sweden. Unemployment ran at 8.7 percent in December.
Sylven estimates some 3,000-4,000 employees could be laid off out of a total of around 16,000 if a merger took place.
Some analysts suggest the state could make the merger conditional, forcing the banks to retain staff. Others see a merger in steps where the banks buy units off the state.
Baird thinks the government could just give the merger a nod and then place their stake in the new bank on the market before any lay-offs have been implemented.

Several analysts have dismissed a previous theory about Investor AB, the key holding company in the Wallenberg family's financial empire, snapping up the state's stake to ensure the Wallenbergs control of the new bank.
The Wallenberg sphere controls 15 percent of S-E-Banken.
The government would rather have an open auction to avoid allegations that it did not get the best price, analysts said.
When speculating about the new bank's structure, analysts think it could be divided into different units to meet various demands of the current customers.
"The bank could be segmented with different names appropriate for the different customers," Sylven said. "The automatic and simple services could be called Nordbanken."
While S-E-Banken handles large companies, investment banking and well-off private individuals, Nordbanken focuses on workers, municipalities and small companies.
S-E-Banken is already segmented to some extent with its investment arm Enskilda and its telephone bank Sesam.

Analysts see Enskilda remaining a part of the new bank and have dismissed rumours about plans to spin it off and list it separately. It is unlikely to get a high valuation in view of the low valuation of many U.S investment banks, they say.
